prompt.context: Our client is the largest European manufacturer of wind turbines (used to generate electricity by harnessing wind power). The client currently has production capability in the US and has elicited your help to determine: 1. Where to build its manufacturing plant? 2. How many plants to build? This problem only concerns North American Operations: wind energy is currently growing in China and the US, but by 2018, there will be capacity issues in the US.
prompt.question: Where should the client build its manufacturing plant(s), and how many plants should it build?

clarifying_info.q: Can the client simply import turbines to the US?
clarifying_info.a: Importing turbines to the US or Asia is impractical because each turbine weighs 80 tons and there are import tariffs that add additional costs.

clarifying_info.q: What is the expected demand for the client's products?
clarifying_info.a: The plant will be online by 2017 and expected demand is 1,500 units, which represents 40% of the market.

clarifying_info.q: What is the market growth rate?
clarifying_info.a: Market growth for the next 5 years is 10% by volume.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the current US competitors?
clarifying_info.a: There are 2 existing US manufacturers of wind turbines with one being the dominant player. There is no differentiation between the different products.

exhibits.title: Relative Effect of Plant Scale on Costs
exhibits.shows: A curve chart showing the relationship between Annual Plant Capacity (x-axis, ranging from 0 to 5000 units) and Cost Per Unit (y-axis). The curve illustrates how cost per unit decreases as plant capacity increases (economies of scale).

data.shape: Downward-sloping curve indicating economies of scale

framework: Demand assessment: estimate current and future market size and client market share to determine capacity needs
Build vs. import analysis: assess feasibility and cost of importing vs. building locally (logistics, tariffs, weight constraints)
Location factors: evaluate supply chain (parts/materials sourcing), proximity to customer demand centers, infrastructure (rail), labor, taxes, and competition
Number of plants: compare economics of one larger plant vs. two smaller plants, including capital cost, operating cost, and transportation savings
Competitive landscape: understand competitor sourcing (Midwest auto supply base), market segmentation, and potential competitive response
China opportunity: assess feasibility of exporting to China given growth there

questions.prompt: Walk through the value chain considerations for where to locate the plant.
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure analysis across: (1) Parts & Material Supply – competitors source from Midwest heavy auto supply base; infrastructure, labor, tax, competition all relevant; (2) Manufacturing – assembly is low-tech mechanical assembly, all engineering design done in Europe, only one turbine type for US production; (3) Transport – finished turbines must be shipped by rail for efficiency; plant should be near demand centers to minimize transport costs; (4) Installation – customers perform their own installation, client provides nominal support; (5) Service – routine maintenance done by independent licensed contractors, fragmented low-barrier market unattractive for client. Location southwest of the Midwest supply base is optimal given proximity to supply and demand (25% West, 50% Central, 25% East market split).

questions.prompt: Using the economies of scale chart, discuss the implications for plant sizing.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that larger plants have lower cost per unit. The client should size the plant to accommodate future growth rather than building minimum capacity today. One larger plant scaled to future demand is more cost-effective than two smaller plants.

questions.prompt: Calculate future demand and determine whether one or two plants are needed. The market in 2018 is 3,750 units; the client holds 40% market share (1,500 units). Market grows 10% per year. A 1,500-unit plant costs $40M ($30M building + $10M equipment). Each additional 500 units of capacity adds $15M. Minimum plant size is 1,500 units. If 2 plants are built, additional operating costs are $15M/year but transportation savings are $7M/year.
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a demand table projecting 40% share of a 10%-growing market from 2018 onward. Client will not reach 3,000 units until ~2025. Therefore only one plant is needed for the foreseeable future. Candidate should compare one-plant vs. two-plant total cost over 8 years to 2025 to confirm.

math.setup: Starting market size 2018: 3,750 units; client share: 40% = 1,500 units. Market grows 10%/year. Target capacity needed by 2025: ~3,000 units (client's 40% of ~7,308 market units). One-plant option: start at 1,500 units capacity, expand incrementally to 3,000 units. Two-plant option: build 2 plants immediately, each 1,500 units = 3,000 units total capacity from day 1, but extra $15M operating cost and $7M transport savings per year.
steps: One plant to 3,000 units capacity: $40M + $15M * 3 additional increments of 500 units = $40M + $45M = $85M total capital
Two plants: $40M * 2 = $80M capital + ($15M operating cost - $7M transport savings) * 8 years = $80M + $8M * 8 = $80M + $64M = $144M total cost
Conclusion: One plant ($85M) vs. two plants ($144M) — one plant is ~$59M cheaper over the period
math.answer: Build one plant sized to reach 3,000 units capacity by 2025, costing ~$85M total. Two plants would cost ~$144M. Client's demand will not reach 3,000 units until 2025, so a single plant with phased capacity additions is optimal.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors should the client consider when choosing the specific location for the plant within the US?

categories.name: Supply chain
ideas: Proximity to Midwest auto supply base (where competitors source parts)

categories.name: Transportation to customers
ideas: Rail access for outbound finished turbines (80-ton units require rail)
Proximity to the Central US market (50% of demand)
Access to West (25%) and East (25%) demand centers

categories.name: Competition
ideas: Avoid overlap with competitor supply networks if possible

recommendation: Build one plant located near but southwest of the Midwest supply base to leverage the existing heavy auto parts supply network while staying close to the largest demand center (Central US, 50% of market)
Size the plant to ultimately accommodate ~3,000 units of capacity (phased expansion), not just the initial 1,500 units, to reduce long-term per-unit costs and avoid a second plant
risks: Competitive response from existing US manufacturers could erode the client's 40% market share assumption
Market growth slower than 10% could delay the need for expanded capacity
Demand concentration in Central US may shift over time, reducing location advantage
next_steps: Conduct detailed site selection analysis in the southwest Midwest corridor (e.g., Kansas, Oklahoma, Missouri)
Model phased capacity expansion timing tied to annual demand milestones
Assess competitive response scenarios and build contingency plans for market share fluctuations
Evaluate potential China export opportunity separately given growing demand there
